newsitem.title: FRANCE: CYCLING-ZABEL STRIPPED OF STAGE WIN IN INCIDENT-RIDDEN SPRINT.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-ZABEL STRIPPED OF STAGE WIN IN INCIDENT-RIDDEN SPRINT.

text.p: Dutchman Jeroen Blijlevens was awarded victory in the sixth stage of the Tour de France on Friday after German Erik Zabel was relegated to last place for dangerous tactics.
Belgian Tom Steels was expelled from the Tour for "violent behaviour" after he threw his bottle at Frenchman Frederic Moncassin in the incident-ridden finish.

Points leader Zabel, winner of Tuesday's stage in Plumelec, appeared to have won the day's honours in impressive fashion, surging through in the last 300 metres of the 217.5-km stage from Le Blanc to Marennes.

But after studying the finish on video the organisers decided Zabel was guilty of "irregular sprinting". They also fined the Telekom rider, winner of the points standings last year, 200 Swiss francs ($140).
Telekom manager Rudy Pevenage said his team would appeal against the decision.
"We're very surprised by this decision because our rider was alone in the last 250 metres and stayed in line throughout the sprint," he said.
Steels' Mapei team have also appealed against the Belgian's disqualification from the Tour.
Blijlevens -- like Steels, a leading sprint specialist -- won Tour stages in 1995 and 1996.
Uzbek Djamolidine Abdoujaparov moved up from third to second place in the stage after the judgment against Zabel.

Frenchman Cedric Vasseur, winner of Thursday's stage after the only succesful breakaway of this Tour, retained the overall leader's yellow jersey but also had a big scare as crashes again marred the race.
He was held up in the second pile-up of the day but managed to catch the leading bunch with the help of his team mates.
"It was a little fright," the GAN rider said.
But it was overwhelmed by the thrill of a lifetime.
"To ride with the yellow jersey on your back is even more exciting than winning it," he said.
"I did not ride a mile without hearing people shout my name. I will never forget it. It was wonderful."
The strong wind on the Atlantic coastline of western France may explain the falls, which spared hardly anyone.
"I fell. There was nothing I could do but the whole team were around me, sheltering me against the wind. I was not worried," Vasseur said.
On Saturday the Tour will reach Bordeaux for a record 75th time. Sprinters have generally won in the famous wine city.
